title: The Homeward Voyage — the Nostos from Troy to Ithaca
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: From Fallen Troy — the Cicones and the Storm at Malea

stops.name: Troy (Ilion) — the wooden horse and the sack
stops.campa: The ten-year war ends by his cunning. Odysseus devises the hollow horse; the Greeks feign departure, and the Trojans haul the wooden beast within their own walls. At night the hidden warriors pour out, the gates are opened, and Ilion burns. Priam falls, the towers topple, the smoke rises to heaven. He gathers his twelve black ships and his Cephallenian men, laden with spoil, and puts out from the smoking citadel toward the sea. Athena, who steered his stratagem, will not yet grant him easy passage; Poseidon's wrath waits offshore. Sacred Ilion has fallen; the long return begins.
stops.quote: Sing to me of the man, Muse, the man of twists and turns driven time and again off course, once he had plundered the hallowed heights of Troy.
suggested_refs: The Trojan Horse relief, Mykonos vase (c. 670 BC)
Tiepolo, The Procession of the Trojan Horse into Troy

stops.name: Ismarus of the Cicones — the sack and the counter-raid
stops.campa: The wind carries him first to Ismarus, city of the Cicones on the Thracian shore. He storms the town, kills the men, takes the women and treasure, and shares the spoil fairly among his crews. He urges swift flight; his men will not obey. They linger on the beach, slaughtering sheep and drinking wine, until the inland Cicones muster at dawn, thick as leaves in spring. The battle turns; six benchmen from each ship are cut down. Only at evening, beaten, do the survivors row clear, grieving for the dead comrades yet glad to have escaped death themselves.
stops.quote: The wind drove me from Ilium to the Cicones, to Ismarus. There I sacked the city and slew the men.
suggested_refs: Attic red-figure depictions of Odysseus at sea

stops.name: Cape Malea — driven from his course
stops.campa: Rounding the southern horn of the Peloponnese at Cape Malea, he is within reach of home. But the North Wind and a great current seize the twelve ships and hurl them past Cythera into the open sea. For nine days the deadly gales drive him across the fish-filled waters, out of all known geography, beyond the maps of men. Here the true wandering begins: from this cape the world of harbors and kingdoms gives way to the world of monsters and enchantresses. Home lies a bowshot behind him and ten years ahead.
stops.quote: But as I was rounding Malea, the wave and current and the North Wind pushed me off course and drove me past Cythera.
suggested_refs: Nautical charts of the Malea current

segments.name: The Wanderings Begin — Lotus, the Cyclops, and the Winds

stops.name: Land of the Lotus-Eaters — Djerba (Meninx)
stops.campa: After nine days of storm he beaches on the shore of the Lotus-Eaters, a gentle people who eat only the honey-sweet lotus flower. He sends three men inland to learn who dwells here. The Lotus-Eaters offer them the fruit, and whoever tastes it forgets his homeward journey, wishing only to stay and browse the lotus forever, all memory of Ithaca dissolved. Odysseus drags the weeping men back by force, binds them beneath the rowing-benches, and commands the rest to embark at once, before any other should eat and lose the will to return. Polybius names this shore Djerba, off Libya.
stops.quote: Whoever ate the honeyed fruit of the lotus lost all desire to send a message back, or return; they wished to stay forever, feeding on lotus, forgetting the way home.

stops.name: The Goat Island off the Cyclopes' coast
stops.campa: He comes to a wooded island lying off the mainland of the Cyclopes, thick with wild goats untouched by hunters, for the Cyclopes have no ships. His crews land and feast; each ship takes nine goats, his own ship ten. From across the water they see smoke and hear the bleating of the giants' flocks and the voices of the one-eyed men. Curious and greedy for guest-gifts, Odysseus chooses to cross with a single ship and twelve chosen men, carrying a skin of the potent dark wine of Maron, priest of Apollo — the wine that will undo the monster.
suggested_refs: Isole Ciclopi (Faraglioni dei Ciclopi), Aci Trezza

stops.name: The Cave of Polyphemus — 'Nobody' and the burning stake
stops.campa: In the giant's cave Polyphemus rolls a stone no twenty wagons could move across the mouth and traps them. He devours two men at a time, dashing their brains on the ground. Odysseus offers the dark wine; the drunken Cyclops asks his name and hears 'Nobody.' As he sleeps, they heat a great olive stake to a glowing point and drive it into his single eye — it hisses like iron in a smith's trough. He roars; the neighbor Cyclopes call, 'Who harms you?' 'Nobody!' — so none come. At dawn the men escape lashed beneath the rams' bellies. Offshore, Odysseus taunts him by name, and the blinded giant prays to Poseidon.
stops.quote: Cyclops, if any man ever asks you who blinded you, say that it was Odysseus, sacker of cities, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.
suggested_refs: Eleusis amphora, Blinding of Polyphemus (c. 650 BC)
Sperlonga sculpture group, Blinding of Polyphemus

stops.name: Aeolia — the island of Aeolus and the bag of winds
stops.campa: He reaches the floating island of Aeolus, ringed with a wall of bronze, where the keeper of the winds feasts with his six sons wed to his six daughters. A month Aeolus hosts him, then gives a parting gift: an ox-hide bag binding all the stormy winds, leaving only the gentle West to blow him home. Nine days they sail; on the tenth the hills of Ithaca rise, so near he sees the fires. He sleeps at last — and his crew, thinking the bag holds gold, open it. The winds burst out and hurl them back to Aeolia, who now drives him off as a man the gods have cursed.
stops.quote: He gave me a bag made of the hide of a nine-year ox, and bound within it the paths of the blustering winds.

stops.name: Telepylus of the Laestrygonians — the fleet destroyed
stops.campa: For six days he rows without rest and comes to Telepylus, the steep-cliffed harbor of the Laestrygonians, where the paths of night and day lie close and a sleepless herdsman might earn double wages. His eleven ships moor within the narrow, land-locked haven; his own alone he ties to a rock outside. Scouts meet the giant king Antiphates, who seizes and eats one on the spot. The Laestrygonians swarm the cliffs and hurl boulders down, spearing the men like fish, smashing every ship in the harbor. Only Odysseus's ship, moored outside, cuts its cable and escapes. Eleven crews are gone; one ship remains of twelve.
stops.quote: The Laestrygonians came thronging from every side, thousands of them, not like men but Giants, and hurled down rocks; a dreadful din arose of dying men and shattering ships.
sources: Victor Bérard, Les Phéniciens et l'Odyssée

stops.name: Aeaea — Circe, the men to swine, the moly
stops.campa: The last ship comes to Aeaea, the island of Circe, daughter of the Sun, weaving at her loom and singing. A scouting party enters her hall; she feeds them drugged food, strikes them with her wand, and they become swine, penned in the sty with the minds of men. Eurylochus flees to warn Odysseus. Hermes meets him on the path and gives him the black-rooted white flower moly, proof against her magic. When her potion fails and her drawn blade meets his own, Circe yields, restores his men, and becomes his host and lover. A full year they feast in her halls before his crew reminds him of home.
stops.quote: She led them in and sat them on chairs, and mixed them cheese and barley and pale honey with Pramnian wine, and drugs; and when they had drunk she struck them with her wand and penned them in the sties. They had the heads and voices, bristles and shape of swine, but their minds were unchanged.

segments.name: The Descent — the Kingdom of the Dead

stops.name: The Grove of Persephone at Ocean's edge — the Cimmerians
stops.campa: Circe sends him to the world's edge, past the stream of Ocean to the land of the Cimmerians, wrapped forever in mist where the Sun never shines. He beaches the ship, and by the meeting of the rivers of the dead — Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, Cocytus — he digs the trench and pours the offerings: milk, honey, wine, water, barley. He cuts the throats of a black ram and ewe; the dark blood fills the pit, and up from Erebus the shades swarm toward it — brides, unwed youths, old men, warriors in bloodied armor — with an eerie cry. He holds them back until Tiresias may drink and speak.
suggested_refs: Cape near the Acheron mouth, Greece

stops.name: The Underworld — the prophecy of Tiresias
stops.campa: The shade of the blind seer Tiresias drinks the black blood and knows him. He foretells the whole return: Poseidon's wrath for the blinded Cyclops; the cattle of the Sun on Thrinacia that must not be touched, or ship and men are lost and he comes home late and alone, on a stranger's ship, to a house of insolent suitors devouring his goods. These he shall kill. Then he must go inland carrying an oar until he meets men who take it for a winnowing-fan, and there plant it and sacrifice to Poseidon; and at last a gentle death shall come from the sea, in sleek old age.
stops.quote: Late shall you come home, in evil plight, with all your comrades lost, in a stranger's ship, and you shall find trouble in your house — proud men devouring your livelihood.
suggested_refs: Attic red-figure pelike, Odysseus and the shades

stops.name: The Underworld — the mother Anticleia and the heroes
stops.campa: His own mother Anticleia drinks the blood and knows her son; she died of longing for him. Three times he tries to embrace her, three times she slips through his arms like a shadow. He sees the great women of old — Tyro, Antiope, Alcmene, Leda, Ariadne — then the heroes: Agamemnon murdered at his homecoming, who warns him of treacherous wives; Achilles, who would rather be a hired serf among the living than king of the dead; sullen Ajax who will not speak; Heracles, and Minos judging, and Sisyphus and Tantalus at their eternal toil. The thronging dead press so thick that he flees to the ship in dread.
stops.quote: By god, I'd rather slave on earth for another man — some dirt-poor tenant farmer who scrapes to keep alive — than rule down here over all the breathless dead.

segments.name: The Perilous Strait — Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis

stops.name: Return to Aeaea — the burial of Elpenor
stops.campa: He sails back across Ocean to Aeaea to bury Elpenor, the youngest crewman, who fell drunk from Circe's roof and broke his neck and whose shade begged in the Underworld not to be left unwept and unburied. They burn his body with his armor, heap a mound, and plant his oar upright upon it. Circe comes down laden with food and wine, and through the night she tells Odysseus each danger that lies ahead: the Sirens, the Wandering Rocks, Scylla and Charybdis, and the forbidden cattle of the Sun. She teaches him how to pass each one alive.
stops.quote: There burn me with all my armour, and heap a mound for me on the shore of the grey sea, that men to come may learn my story; and plant upon the mound the oar I rowed with among my fellows.

stops.name: The Wandering Rocks (Planctae) — the path not taken
stops.campa: Circe set two routes before him beyond the Sirens. One passes the Wandering Rocks, the Planctae, sheer cliffs the blue swell smashes against, where no ship of men has ever slipped through — only Argo, beloved of Hera, once came by, and even her the waves would have dashed but for the goddess. Over these rocks even the timid doves that carry ambrosia to Zeus are lost, one each time, so that the Father must always add another to keep the number. Warned that this way means certain wreck, Odysseus chooses the other channel — the narrow strait guarded by Scylla and Charybdis.
stops.quote: No ship of men that comes there ever escapes, but the waves of the sea and storms of ruinous fire carry away together the planks of ships and bodies of men.
suggested_refs: The Aeolian Islands and their volcanic stacks
Argo among the Symplegades, ancient vase-painting

stops.name: The Island of the Sirens — bound to the mast
stops.campa: As Circe warned, he plugs his crew's ears with kneaded beeswax and has them lash him upright to the mast, ordering that if he begs to be freed they must only bind him tighter. The wind drops; the sea goes glassy still. From their flowered meadow, heaped with the bones of rotting men, the Sirens sing — promising knowledge of all that happens on the earth, the whole tale of Troy. His heart bursts with longing; he strains at the ropes and signals to be loosed. But Perimedes and Eurylochus only bind him faster, and the rowers pull until the deadly voices fade behind them.
stops.quote: Come hither, renowned Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans; stop your ship that you may listen to our voices. No man has ever rowed past this isle without hearing the honey-sweet song from our lips.

stops.name: Scylla and Charybdis — the Strait of Messina
stops.campa: He enters the narrow strait between two cliffs. On one side, under a wild fig-tree, divine Charybdis three times a day sucks down the black sea and belches it back, a whirlpool no ship survives. On the other, in a cave high in the rock, six-necked Scylla thrusts out her heads, each with a triple row of teeth, and snatches men from passing ships. Circe bade him hug Scylla's cliff rather than lose all. As he steers close, Scylla darts down and seizes six of his best men; he sees them lifted writhing overhead, calling his name — the most piteous sight of all his sufferings at sea.
stops.quote: Scylla snatched from the hollow ship six of my companions, the best in strength of hand. Looking into the swift ship I saw their feet and hands as they were lifted up on high, and they cried aloud, calling on me by name for that last time in anguish of heart.
suggested_refs: Fresco of Scylla, House of the Vettii (resonance)

segments.name: The Cattle of the Sun and the Loss of the Ship

stops.name: Thrinacia — the cattle of Helios devoured
stops.campa: They come to Thrinacia, the island of the Sun, where Helios pastures his deathless golden cattle, seven herds and seven flocks, tended by his daughters. Tiresias and Circe both forbade them; Odysseus makes his men swear to touch no beast. But contrary winds pen them a month; the provisions fail; hunger gnaws. While he sleeps, Eurylochus persuades the starving crew to slaughter the finest cattle and feast. Helios, enraged, demands justice of Zeus, threatening to shine among the dead. The flayed hides crawl and the meat lows on the spits. Six days they feast; on the seventh they sail, and Zeus's thunderbolt shatters the ship.
stops.quote: You will reach the island of Thrinacia. There the cattle of the Sun graze, and his fat sheep. If you leave them unharmed you may still reach Ithaca, though in hardship; but if you harm them, then I foretell the ruin of your ship and your men.
suggested_refs: Mount Etna and the Sicilian plains

stops.name: The wreck and the second passing of Charybdis
stops.campa: The thunderbolt splits the ship; the crew are flung into the sea and drown, denied their homecoming, as Helios willed. Odysseus alone survives, clinging to the lashed keel and mast. The wind drives him back toward Charybdis. As the whirlpool sucks his makeshift raft down, he leaps and clings to the fig-tree on the cliff above like a bat, hanging until the timbers are spat up again; then he drops onto them and paddles clear with his hands. Nine days he drifts alone on the wide sea, the last man of twelve ships, until the current carries him to a distant island.
stops.quote: So I was borne along for nine days, and on the tenth night the gods brought me to the island of Ogygia.
suggested_refs: Ancient depictions of Odysseus on a raft

segments.name: The Nymph's Island — Seven Years with Calypso

stops.name: Ogygia — Calypso, seven years, immortality refused
stops.campa: The lone survivor washes up on Ogygia, the island of the nymph Calypso, in her cave hung with vines amid alder, poplar and cypress, four springs and soft meadows of violet. She takes him as her own, tends him, and would make him her immortal husband, ageless and deathless forever. Seven years she keeps him. Yet each day he sits on the shore weeping, gazing over the barren sea toward Ithaca, his heart broken with longing for home and wife. He refuses immortality: he would rather see the smoke leaping from his own hearth and then die. At last Zeus sends Hermes, and weeping Calypso must let him go.
stops.quote: Full well I know that wise Penelope is meaner to look upon than you in comeliness and stature... yet even so I wish and long day by day to reach my home, and to see the day of my return.

stops.name: The raft and the storm of Poseidon
stops.campa: Calypso gives him tools; in four days he builds a broad raft, and on the fifth she sends him off with a fair wind, bread, wine and water. Seventeen days he sails by the stars she taught him, keeping the Bear on his left hand. On the eighteenth the mountains of the Phaeacians rise like a shield on the misty sea. But Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, rouses a monstrous storm; wave upon wave shatters the raft. The sea-goddess Ino Leucothea gives him her immortal veil; he swims two days and nights, and Athena stills the winds, until half-dead he grasps the rocks of a river-mouth and crawls ashore.
stops.quote: Keep the Great Bear on your left hand as you cross the sea.

segments.name: The Court of the Phaeacians — the Tale Told at the Feast

stops.name: The river-mouth of Scheria — Nausicaa on the shore
stops.campa: Naked, crusted with brine, he wakes in the bushes to girls' laughter. The princess Nausicaa has come with her maids to wash linen at the river and play at ball. When their cry startles her companions to flight, she alone stands her ground. He supplicates her, hiding his nakedness with a branch, comparing her to Artemis and to a young palm-shoot he once saw at Delos. She gives him clothing, food and oil, and directs him to her father's palace — but bids him follow at a distance, lest the townsfolk gossip. Athena wraps him in mist and grace as he goes up to the city of Alcinous.
stops.quote: I never saw such a mortal, man or woman — wonder holds me as I look on you... in Delos once I saw a young palm-shoot springing near Apollo's altar; and I marveled at it so.
suggested_refs: Ermones beach and the Nausicaa site

stops.name: The palace of Alcinous — the tale told, the ship home
stops.campa: In the bronze-walled hall of King Alcinous, its gardens bearing fruit in every season, he is received as a guest before his name is known. At the feast the blind bard Demodocus sings of the wooden horse, and the stranger weeps behind his cloak. Pressed, he reveals himself: 'I am Odysseus,' and tells the whole tale of his wanderings — the Cyclops, Circe, the dead, the Sirens, Scylla, the Sun's cattle, Calypso — to the spellbound court. Laden with gifts, he is put aboard a Phaeacian ship that sails so swiftly it lands him sleeping on his own Ithacan shore. Poseidon, in fury, turns the ship to stone.
stops.quote: I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known before all men for the study of crafty designs, and my fame goes up to the heavens.
suggested_refs: Pontikonisi (Mouse Island) — the petrified Phaeacian ship
Palaiokastritsa, said site of the palace

segments.name: Ithaca — the Homecoming and the Slaughter of the Suitors

stops.name: The cave of the nymphs, Ithaca — landed home at last
stops.campa: The Phaeacians lay him sleeping on the beach of Phorcys with all his treasure and depart. He wakes and does not know his own land, for Athena has poured a mist over it. When she lifts it and reveals the harbor, the olive by the cave of the naiads, the mountain Neriton, he kisses the earth of his home. The goddess appears and they take counsel together, hiding the gifts in the cave. She disguises him: withers his skin, dims his eyes, dresses him in a beggar's rags, that he may test his household and destroy the suitors unrecognized. Twenty years he has been gone.
stops.quote: Then Odysseus rejoiced, glad at the sight of his own country, and he kissed the earth, the giver of grain.

stops.name: The hut of Eumaeus — the faithful swineherd
stops.campa: Disguised as an old beggar, he climbs to the steading of Eumaeus the swineherd, faithful servant on the rocky heights. The dogs rush him; Eumaeus drives them off and welcomes the stranger, slaughtering a pig, sharing his rough fare and his own bitter grief for a master he believes long dead — cursing the suitors who waste his lord's estate. Odysseus, testing him, invents a Cretan life-story. Here Athena brings Telemachus, newly returned from Pylos and Sparta, safe past the suitors' ambush. Father and son are left alone; Odysseus reveals himself, and they weep and clasp each other, and begin to plot the suitors' doom.
stops.quote: I long for Odysseus, who is gone. Even in his absence, friend, I am ashamed to speak his name, for he loved and cared for me greatly.
suggested_refs: Marathia plateau (traditional site of Eumaeus's steading)
Ancient depictions of Odysseus in disguise

stops.name: The steading reunion — father and son revealed
stops.campa: While Eumaeus is sent to tell Penelope her son is safe, Athena restores Odysseus to his full stature and beauty in the hut, and he stands transfigured before Telemachus. The young man shrinks back, thinking him a god. 'No god am I,' says Odysseus, 'I am your father, for whom you have grieved twenty years.' Telemachus at first cannot believe it; then they fall into each other's arms and weep aloud, crying shrill and thick as birds robbed of their young. Tearless at last, they count the suitors — over a hundred — and plan: hide the hall's weapons, tell no one, endure every insult, and wait for the sign of Zeus.
stops.quote: I am your father, for whose sake you grieve and suffer many pains, bowing beneath the violence of men.
suggested_refs: Odysseus and Telemachus reunited, Henri-Lucien Doucet

stops.name: The palace threshold — the dog Argos knows his master
stops.campa: He goes down to his own hall as a beggar. At the gate lies Argos, the hunting-dog he reared as a pup twenty years before, now old and neglected, covered in vermin on a heap of dung. Alone of all Ithaca the dog knows him instantly: he cannot rise, but he droops his ears and wags his tail. Odysseus, keeping his disguise, turns aside a secret tear. And Argos, having seen his master again in the twentieth year, is taken by the darkness of death. Within, the suitors mock and abuse the beggar; Antinous hurls a stool at him. Odysseus endures, storing up wrath.
stops.quote: But the fate of black death seized Argos straightway, when he had seen Odysseus in the twentieth year.
suggested_refs: Argos and Odysseus, ancient and modern illustrations

stops.name: The washing of the feet — the scar and Eurycleia
stops.campa: That evening Penelope, moved by the beggar's bearing, bids the old nurse Eurycleia wash the stranger's feet. She reared Odysseus from infancy; as she cradles his leg she finds the long white scar above the knee, torn by a boar's tusk when he hunted on Parnassus with his grandfather Autolycus. She knows him at once; the basin overturns, the water spills, joy and grief seize her, and her eyes brim. She looks to Penelope to tell — but Odysseus grips her throat and swears her to silence: the hour is not yet. She keeps the secret, and the poet turns aside to sing how he first got the wound.
stops.quote: Surely you are Odysseus, dear child, and I did not know you, till I had handled all the body of my lord.
suggested_refs: Eurycleia washing Odysseus's feet, Attic red-figure skyphos (Chiusi, c. 440 BC)

stops.name: The contest of the bow — the string no other can draw
stops.campa: Penelope, testing the suitors, sets Odysseus's great back-strung bow before them: whoever can string it and shoot an arrow clean through the sockets of twelve axe-heads shall have her. One after another the strong young suitors strain and fail; they warm and grease the bow, yet none can bend it. The beggar asks to try. Amid their jeers Telemachus grants it. He handles the bow like a bard fitting a new string to his lyre, strings it effortlessly, plucks the cord so it sings like a swallow, and drives the arrow straight through all twelve axes without a miss. Zeus thunders. The hour of vengeance has come.
stops.quote: As when a man skilled in the lyre and in song easily stretches a new string round a peg... so without effort did Odysseus string the great bow. Then he plucked the string, and it sang sweetly beneath his hand, like the voice of a swallow.
suggested_refs: The axe-heads and bow contest, Greek vase-painting
Odysseus stringing the bow, N.C. Wyeth illustration

stops.name: The hall of slaughter — the suitors destroyed
stops.campa: He leaps to the great threshold, pours the arrows out at his feet, and throws off his rags. 'Now for another mark no man has hit!' — and shoots Antinous through the throat as he lifts the wine-cup. He names himself, and terror seizes the suitors; the doors are barred, Athena's aegis flashes overhead. With Telemachus, Eumaeus and the cowherd he cuts them down — arrows, then spears — until the whole hall is heaped with the dead, fallen in blood and dust like fish poured out on the sand. The faithless maids are hanged; the traitor Melanthius is butchered. He purges the hall with fire and sulphur.
stops.quote: You dogs! you never thought I would return from Troy, and so you wasted my house, and lay with my women by force, and wooed my wife while I still lived, fearing neither the gods nor the vengeance of men. Now the day of your doom is come.
suggested_refs: The slaying of the suitors, Campanian and Attic vase-painting
Odysseus and the suitors, Thomas Degeorge (1812)

stops.name: The bridal chamber — the secret of the olive-tree bed
stops.campa: Penelope, cautious after twenty years and many false tales, will not yet believe. To test him she bids the nurse move their marriage bed outside the chamber. Odysseus flares in anger — for he built that bed himself, carving the bedpost from the living trunk of an olive-tree still rooted in the earth, and framing the room around it; no man could move it unless he cut the root. Only he and she and one maid ever knew the secret. Hearing it, Penelope's knees and heart give way; she runs weeping to embrace him. Athena holds back the dawn to lengthen their night, and at last, home and known, they sleep.
stops.quote: There is a great secret in the making of this bed. I built it myself, and no other man. A branching olive-tree grew inside the court... about this I built my chamber, and I cut away the crown of the olive, and I fashioned the bedpost from the stump.
suggested_refs: Penelope and Odysseus reunited, Francesco Primaticcio fresco
The olive-tree bed motif in Renaissance painting

stops.name: The orchard of Laertes — the tree-count and the peace
stops.campa: At dawn he climbs to the country farm where old Laertes, worn with grief, toils in his vineyard in a patched tunic. Odysseus tests him with a false name, then, seeing his father heap dust on his white head, can bear no more: he shows the boar-scar and names the very trees Laertes gave him as a boy — thirteen pears, ten apples, forty figs, the ordered rows of vines. The old man's knees give way; they embrace. But the suitors' kinsmen rise in arms. Laertes, his strength renewed by Athena, casts the first spear and kills Eupeithes. Then Zeus hurls a thunderbolt; Athena commands peace, and Ithaca is quiet.
stops.quote: These trees you gave me long ago, when I asked you for them, being but a child, following you through the garden; and you named them each to me.
suggested_refs: Odysseus and Laertes in the orchard, 19th-century engravings
